person.name: Konrad_Zuse
person.summary: Konrad Zuse was a German engineer and inventor who built the Z3, an operational programmable computer, in Berlin during World War II. He also developed the Plankalkül programming language and founded Zuse KG, one of Germany's first computer companies.

conclusion: The Z3 was later reconstructed for museum display. Historians of computing study it as an early fully functional programmable computer. Plankalkül remains part of the history of programming-language design.

events.title: Born Into a Postal Household
events.description: Konrad Zuse was born in Deutsch-Wilmersdorf, Berlin, to Maria and Emil Zuse. Emil Zuse worked as a mid-level postal official, and Konrad entered a household that already included an older sister.

events.title: Schooling Across Prussia
events.description: In 1912, Konrad Zuse moved with Maria and Emil Zuse from Deutsch-Wilmersdorf to Braunsberg, where Emil worked as a postal official. Zuse attended the Hosianum Gymnasium there. The family moved to Hoyerswerda in 1923, and he attended the Reform-Realgymnasium before completing school in 1928.

events.title: Earns a Civil Engineering Diploma
events.description: In 1935, Konrad Zuse completed his civil-engineering diploma at the Technical University of Berlin. He had first studied mechanical engineering and architecture. He also spent nearly a year working as an advertising illustrator.

events.title: Opens Home Workshop
events.description: In 1935, Konrad Zuse left his job as a structural engineer at Henschel Aircraft Works in Schönefeld near Berlin. He established an inventor’s workshop in his parents’ Berlin apartment and began developing the [[Z1|Z1 programmable calculating machine]] to automate repetitive engineering calculations.

Z1.explanation: The Z1 was Zuse’s electrically powered mechanical calculating machine. It used binary numbers and included separate input, output, calculation, memory, and program units, although it did not operate reliably.

events.background:
Zuse’s parents became the first financial base for the work. His father, Emil Zuse, came out of retirement to help pay for it. Other people also contributed money or labor after he persuaded them with his enthusiasm. The apartment project continued habits formed long before his engineering career. At fourteen, he devised a coin-operated mandarin dispenser that returned change. At eighteen, he assembled a coal-loading crane from a Stabil metal construction set. The manufacturer awarded him an honorary certificate for the crane.

By June 1937, his diary described his preoccupation with a “mechanical brain.” He had independently rediscovered propositional logic while working on his first computer designs. He learned of Charles Babbage only long after World War II. Zuse later called Babbage the true father of the computer. The first design also gave him a way to represent numbers for machine calculation with a mantissa and an exponent. Modern computers still use this general approach for floating-point numbers.

Mechanical precision created a stubborn practical problem. The machine’s mechanical switching parts repeatedly jammed, so calculations could not run dependably. While work continued, Zuse transferred its circuit ideas into electromechanical relays. He tested that approach with fixed-point numbers in the Z2 prototype, completed in 1939. In 1940 he demonstrated the Z2 to Günther Bock, technical director of the German Aviation Research Institute. Bock agreed to finance the next machine’s development.

events.title: Completes the Mechanical Z1 Computer
events.description: In 1938, Konrad Zuse completed the Z1 in his parents' Berlin apartment. The machine used mechanical parts and did not operate reliably. Helmut Schreyer collaborated with Zuse during this period.

event_class.title: Z1
event_class.description: An electrically driven mechanical computer uses binary numbers, punched-film programs, separate memory, and arithmetic units to automate engineering calculations.
event_class.impact: Its design supplies the basic structure Zuse carries into his later relay computers.

events.title: Forms Berlin Engineering Office
events.description: In 1941, Konrad Zuse established Zuse Engineering Office and Apparatus Construction in Berlin. The office employed a staff of up to 20 people. German aviation institutions and armaments businesses funded its computing work during the war.

events.title: Presents the Programmable Z3 Computer
events.description: On May 12, 1941, Konrad Zuse presented the Z3, a relay-based programmable computer, in Berlin with Helmut Schreyer. The [[German Aeronautical Research Institute|German aviation research organization]] had supported its completion for aeronautical calculations.

German Aeronautical Research Institute.explanation: Germany's main aviation-research organization supported technical work for aircraft development. Its director Günther Bock helped finance the Z3 after seeing an earlier Zuse machine.

event_class.title: Z3
event_class.description: An electromechanical computer uses telephone relays, binary floating-point arithmetic, memory, and punched-film instructions to execute automatically programmed calculations.
event_class.impact: It becomes operational as the first functional freely programmable computer.

events.background:
Civil-engineering calculations had given Zuse the original problem. He found the routine structural work monotonous and laborious, then left his job in 1935 to build machines in his parents’ apartment. The Z1, completed in 1938, used mechanically moving parts that regularly jammed because the required precision was hard to maintain. Its program reader used perforated movie film. Zuse transferred its design to relays for the Z2, a smaller test machine completed in 1939. Bock saw that machine in 1940 and agreed to fund further work.

Schreyer had already urged a faster path. In 1938, he and Zuse presented an experimental circuit at the Technical University of Berlin that used vacuum tubes in place of relays. Their proposal for an electronic calculating machine was dismissed there as “fantasy.” Schreyer continued work on tube circuits while serving as an assistant at the university’s Institute for Oscillation Research. He completed a 1941 dissertation titled The Tube Relay and Its Circuit Technology. The institute belonged to the Four Year Plan administration’s network of roughly 30 scientific institutes and had to conduct military research.

The machine’s immediate practical use lay in aircraft research. It calculated a complex matrix for investigations of wing flutter, the dangerous vibration that had caused many aircraft crashes. The work was tied to Zuse’s wartime employment at Henschel Aircraft Works, where he also helped develop special calculators for measuring the wings of the Hs 293 glide bomb. His engineering office eventually employed 20 people. Armaments firms and Nazi institutions financed Zuse’s computer work with more than 250,000 Reichsmarks.

The original machine was destroyed in an air raid on December 21, 1943. A working exhibition replica was built by Zuse KG in 1962 and is held by the Deutsches Museum in Munich. In 1998, Raúl Rojas found that joining the perforated tape into a loop could give the machine the capabilities of a universal computer.

events.title: Designs the Plankalkül Language
events.description: During World War II in Berlin, Konrad Zuse designed Plankalkül, a formal language for writing algorithms independently of a particular machine. He developed it while working on the Z4, his next relay computer. Wartime conditions kept the design unpublished.

event_class.title: Plankalkül
event_class.description: A formal programming language uses typed variables, assignment statements, and structured operations to express algorithms independently of a particular machine.
event_class.impact: Its concepts anticipate elements later used in high-level programming languages.

events.title: Flees Berlin With the Z4
events.description: As the war ended in 1945, Konrad Zuse fled Berlin with Gisela Brandes, their family, and colleagues. They traveled through Göttingen to the Allgäu with the partly completed Z4 relay computer. In Hinterstein, Zuse and his team reassembled the machine.

events.title: Marries Gisela Brandes
events.description: On January 6, 1945, Konrad Zuse married Gisela Brandes in Berlin. They married during the final months of World War II.

events.title: Founds Zuse KG
events.description: In 1949, Konrad Zuse founded Zuse KG in Neukirchen in Hesse. Eduard Stiefel arranged for ETH Zurich to rent the Z4. The rental brought funds to the new company.

events.title: Installs the Z4 at ETH Zurich
events.description: In July 1950, Konrad Zuse installed the Z4 at ETH Zurich, the Swiss Federal Institute of Technology, under a rental agreement arranged with Eduard Stiefel. Researchers used the programmable computer for numerical work. Its calculations included work on a dam project.
events.background:
ETH Zurich’s Institute for Applied Mathematics had opened in 1948 under Stiefel’s direction. Its researchers needed machinery for numerical mathematics, where long calculations in engineering and science were commonly carried out by hand or with desk calculators. The Z4 gave the institute the first programmable calculating machine at a continental European university. It was the only functioning computer in Central Europe at the time. Its service began several months before UNIVAC was installed in the United States.

The machine used electromechanical relays, which opened and closed electrical circuits like telephone switches. Programs and data were prepared for the machine’s work. During its five years at ETH, the Z4 handled 55 commissioned jobs and mathematical investigations. The work included calculations for the gravity wall of a dam. A gravity dam holds back water chiefly through its own weight, so engineers had to calculate forces across its heavy masonry or concrete structure. The record of the Z4’s work at ETH also preserves the names of institute staff and surviving witnesses from the period.

Stiefel’s institute used the experience to prepare its own electronic computer, ERMETH. He sent assistants Heinz Rutishauser and Ambros Speiser to the United States to study calculating machines. ERMETH operated at ETH from 1955 through 1963. The Zuse company also built the M9 calculation punch for Swiss Remington Rand. ETH used the M9 in administration, industry, and research. The Z4 later went to the French military research institute ISL in 1955, where it served mainly in ballistic research until 1959.

events.title: Leaves Zuse KG
events.description: In 1964, delivery delays for the Z25 computer left Zuse KG heavily indebted. Konrad Zuse gave up his ownership shares and left active management. He then worked as a consultant.

events.title: Publishes a Computing-Universe Book
events.description: In 1969, Konrad Zuse published Rechnender Raum. The book treated the universe as a giant computing machine. It used a model in which simple cells change according to fixed rules to explore cosmology, the study of the universe.

events.title: Death in Hünfeld
events.description: In retirement, Konrad Zuse painted in an expressionist style. He died in Hünfeld on December 18, 1995, at age 85.
